record.field: Detailed schedule of cash and cash equivalents per reporting date
General ledger and subledger details for all cash accounts.
Bank reconciliation statements as of the reporting date (including outstanding checks, deposits in transit, and reconciling items).
Petty cash count sheets and supporting vouchers.
Company policies regarding cash management, petty cash, and classification of cash equivalents.
Cash receipts and disbursement vouchers (for sample testing).
Bank statements covering the reporting date and subsequent period.
Deposit slips, withdrawal slips, and check copies for significant transactions near year-end (cut-off testing).
Investment certificates or confirmations for term deposits, money market funds, or other cash equivalents.
Bank confirmations from all financial institutions where the company holds accounts
Third-party confirmations for cash equivalents held with brokers, trustees, or other custodians.
Cut-off testing:bank statement (bank transactions after reporting date, usually 7–10 days) to verify reconciling items.
Roll-forward analysis of cash balances (beginning balance + receipts – payments = ending balance).
Cash flow analysis (compare cash movements to operating results for reasonableness).
Review of restricted cash (e.g., deposits held as collateral, escrow accounts).
Foreign currency cash balances → check translation rates and revaluation.
Detailed aged trade receivable listing as of the reporting date (showing customer balances, aging buckets, and total).
General ledger and subsidiary ledger details of trade receivables.
Reconciliation between subledger and general ledger balances.
Company policies on credit sales, allowance for doubtful accounts, and write-offs.
Sales invoices and supporting delivery documents (proof of shipment, customer acceptance) to verify occurrence.
Sales contracts or purchase orders from customers.
Credit memos, debit memos, and journal entries affecting receivable balances.
Subsequent cash receipts records (collections after reporting date) to test collectability.
Correspondence with customers about disputes, returns, or payment arrangements.
Direct confirmations sent to customers (positive or negative confirmations, depending on risk and balance size).
Alternative procedures if confirmations are not returned: check subsequent payments, shipping documents, or contracts.
Aging analysis of receivables (to identify overdue balances and assess collectability).
Subsequent cash collection testing (to validate existence and valuation).
Allowance for expected credit loss (ECL) or bad debts calculation (and management’s assumptions).
Trend analysis (days sales outstanding, turnover ratio, comparison with prior years).
Large or unusual balances → detailed review of supporting contracts and history.
Detailed schedule of contract assets per end of reporting period, reconcilable to the general ledger.
List of customer contracts that give rise to contract assets
Supporting calculation of contract asset balances
Reconciliation between contract assets and revenue recognized.
Accounting policies and judgments used in revenue recognition (e.g., measure of progress, allocation of transaction price).
Changes in estimates (e.g., expected variable consideration, modifications of contracts).
Breakdown by age or category (e.g., short-term vs long-term contract assets).
Invoices and billing schedules compared to contract asset balances.
Evidence of work performed / milestones achieved (e.g., project progress reports, engineering certifications, timesheets, completion certificates).
Adjustments for variable consideration (e.g., rebates, bonuses, penalties).
Management approvals for revenue recognition entries.
Contracts modifications or change orders that affect the calculation of contract assets.
Customer confirmations (similar to receivable confirmations), especially for unbilled revenue tied to delivered work.
Independent certification of project progress (common in construction/long-term contracts).
Roll-forward analysis of contract assets (beginning balance, additions, transfers to receivables, write-offs, ending balance).
Comparison of contract asset balances to prior periods and to revenue trends.
Subsequent billing and collections after the balance sheet date — testing realizability.
Cut-off testing: ensuring contract asset recognition is consistent with progress at year-end.
Assessment of credit risk and expected credit losses (ECL) related to contract assets.
Detailed schedule of financial assets (short-term and long-term)
General ledger and subledger supporting balances.
Accounting policies for classification and measurement.
Roll-forward of financial assets (beginning balance, purchases, disposals, fair value changes, impairment, ending balance).
Management’s impairment assessment / Expected Credit Loss (ECL) model for debt instruments.
Evidence of significant judgments or estimates (e.g., fair value hierarchy, assumptions used in valuation).
Share certificates, bond certificates, or custody/brokerage statements as evidence of ownership.
Loan agreements (if the entity provides financing).
Minutes of Board/Management approval for major investments.
Broker or custodian confirmations (confirming holdings, cost, fair value, restrictions).
Bank confirmations for deposits and investment balances.
Market data from independent pricing sources (Bloomberg, Reuters, stock exchange prices, yield curves).
Valuation reports from external appraisers (for unlisted or complex securities).
Fair value calculations and supporting inputs (interest rates, market multiples, discounted cash flow assumptions).
Interest/dividend income schedules (reconciliation of expected vs. recorded).
Testing for impairment indicators (credit downgrades, default, decline in market value).
Subsequent events review → sales after year-end, credit events, or changes in fair value.
Analysis of investment returns vs. benchmarks for reasonableness.
Detailed listing of all derivative contracts at the reporting date:
General ledger and subsidiary ledger details related to derivatives.
Accounting policies for derivatives (e.g., hedge accounting vs. held for trading).
Master agreements (e.g., ISDA agreements with counterparties).
Trade tickets or deal confirmations for derivative transactions.
Bank or broker statements confirming derivative positions and valuations.
Settlement records for derivatives that matured or were closed out during the year.
Confirmations from counterparties (positive confirmations to verify existence, terms, and valuation).
Independent market data (e.g., interest rates, FX rates, commodity prices, volatility) to validate fair value calculations.
Third-party valuation reports (if obtained by management).
Auditor’s own valuation models (independent recalculation using market inputs).
Roll-forward of derivative balances: beginning balance, new contracts, settlements, fair value changes, ending balance.
Testing of unrealized gains/losses recognized in profit or loss or OCI.
Assessment of hedge effectiveness (if hedge accounting is applied).
Review of management’s assumptions in valuation models (discount rates, volatility, correlations).
Detailed inventory listing (by SKU, product line, or location) as of the reporting date.
General ledger and subsidiary ledger balances for inventory.
Inventory valuation reports, including cost methods (FIFO, weighted average, standard cost, etc.).
Reconciliation between physical counts, perpetual records, and general ledger.
Policies and procedures for inventory costing, valuation, and write-downs.
Purchase invoices and receiving reports for raw materials.
Production records (bill of materials, job cost sheets, labor/machine hours).
Cost accumulation records (overhead allocations, standard vs. actual cost variances).
Shipping documents and sales invoices for goods sold near year-end (cut-off testing).
Inventory write-down documentation (e.g., slow-moving, damaged, or obsolete items).
Inventory tags or count sheets prepared during physical stock counts.
Third-party confirmations for inventory held at external warehouses, consignees, or public storage.
Independent price quotations or market data to validate net realizable value (NRV).
Reconciliation of test counts to client’s inventory records.
Inventory roll-forward: beginning balance, purchases/production, cost of goods sold, adjustments, ending balance.
Aging analysis of inventory (to identify obsolete or slow-moving items).
Gross margin analysis → comparison of current year vs. prior year trends.
Inventory turnover ratios (to test reasonableness of balances).
Standard cost variance analysis (if standard costing is used).
Detailed schedule of prepayments at the reporting date
General ledger and subsidiary ledger balances for prepayments.
Reconciliation between prepayment schedule and general ledger.
Company’s accounting policy for recognizing and amortizing prepayments.
Payment vouchers, bank transfer records, or receipts evidencing the advance payment.
Contracts or agreements that define the coverage period and nature of services/goods (e.g., rental contract, insurance policy, service agreements).
Invoices from vendors supporting the prepaid amounts.
Management’s amortization schedule showing allocation of prepaid amounts to expense over time.
Confirmations from suppliers/service providers (if significant) to validate prepaid balances (e.g., for large rental or insurance contracts).
Subsequent invoices or services received after reporting date to confirm that benefits are being delivered.
Roll-forward of prepayment balances (opening balance, additions, amortizations, closing balance).
Trend analysis: compare current year prepayments to prior year balances to identify unusual fluctuations.
Reasonableness test: check if amortization matches the benefit period (e.g., 12-month insurance policy → 1/12 per month expensed).
Cut-off testing: ensure payments made near year-end are recorded in the correct accounting period.
Detailed schedule of prepaid taxes at the reporting date
General ledger and subsidiary ledger balances of prepaid taxes.
Reconciliation between tax records and general ledger.
Company’s tax policies and calculations, including recognition of prepaid tax versus tax expense.
Tax payment receipts from tax authorities (e.g., proof of income tax installments, VAT payments).
Withholding tax certificates received from customers or other parties.
Tax returns filed (monthly, quarterly, annual), along with supporting schedules.
Correspondence with tax authorities regarding overpayments, refunds, or disputes.
Internal calculations showing how prepaid taxes were determined and applied.
Confirmation or acknowledgment from tax authorities (if available) regarding prepaid balances or refunds.
Subsequent utilization: evidence that prepaid taxes were offset against tax payable in the following year.
Refund approval letters from tax authorities (if refunds are expected).
Roll-forward of prepaid tax balances (opening → additions → applications/refunds → ending).
Comparison of current year vs. prior year prepaid tax balances, considering profit levels and tax rates.
Subsequent events review: confirm if prepaid taxes have been used or refunded after the reporting date.
Detailed breakdown of Other Current Assets as of the reporting date
General ledger and subsidiary ledger balances of OCA.
Reconciliation between subledgers (if any) and the general ledger.
Accounting policies applied to the different categories of items classified under OCA.
Payment vouchers, receipts, or bank records supporting advances and deposits.
Employee advance request forms and clearance reports for employee receivables.
Contracts, agreements, or deposit slips supporting security deposits or guarantees.
Insurance claim documents (if recoverables are included).
Tax documentation (e.g., VAT/input tax claims pending credit or refund).
Loan agreements for short-term loans receivable from third parties or related parties.
Confirmations from counterparties (e.g., for deposits, loans, advances given, or insurance claims).
Acknowledgments from employees for employee advances.
Tax authority confirmations (if OCA includes tax refunds or credits receivable).
Subsequent settlement evidence (cash receipts, offsets, or refunds after reporting date).
Roll-forward analysis: opening balance → additions → utilizations/write-offs → closing balance.
Trend analysis: compare balances with prior years to identify unusual increases or changes.
Subsequent events testing: review payments/settlements after reporting date for realizability.
Reasonableness testing: check whether balances are in line with business practices (e.g., deposits proportional to leases, advances proportional to payroll).
Detailed schedule of non-trade receivables at the reporting date, broken down by category (e.g., employee advances, related-party balances, insurance claims, tax refunds, loans).
General ledger and subsidiary ledger balances of non-trade receivables.
Reconciliation between subsidiary ledger and general ledger.
Company’s accounting policy for recognition, impairment, and write-offs of non-trade receivables.
Employee advance request forms, settlement reports, and payroll deductions (for employee receivables).
Contracts, loan agreements, or promissory notes (for loans and advances to third parties or related parties).
Board of Directors’ approval or shareholder resolutions (if receivables involve related parties).
Tax documentation (for VAT/input tax refunds or other tax-related receivables).
Payment vouchers and bank transfer records supporting advances or deposits.
Confirmations from counterparties (e.g., related parties, borrowers, or insurance companies) to validate balances.
Acknowledgment letters from employees confirming amounts owed (for significant advances).
Tax authority acknowledgments or confirmation for tax refunds/credits receivable.
Subsequent cash receipts evidence (collection or settlement after the reporting date).
Roll-forward of non-trade receivables (opening → additions → collections/write-offs → closing).
Aging analysis of non-trade receivables to evaluate collectability.
Comparison with prior year balances to identify unusual increases or changes.
Reasonableness tests: check if balances align with normal business practices (e.g., size of employee advances or loans to related parties).
Subsequent events review: determine if receivables were realized after year-end.
Detailed schedule of investments in associates
General ledger and subsidiary ledger balances for investment in associates.
Reconciliation of investment balances with supporting schedules.
Company’s accounting policy for recognition, measurement, and impairment of associates.
Investment agreements, purchase contracts, or share certificates proving ownership.
Board of Directors’ resolutions/approvals of the investment.
Associate’s audited financial statements (used to apply equity method).
Management’s calculation of the investor’s share of profit/loss and other comprehensive income.
Impairment assessment documentation (if carrying value may exceed recoverable amount).
Confirmations from the associate of ownership percentage, balances, and transactions.
Public filings or registry extracts (if the associate is publicly listed or registered with authorities).
Market data (if fair value is disclosed in notes or required).
Comparison of investor’s recorded share of associate’s results with underlying financial statements of the associate.
Trend analysis: assess consistency of associate’s performance vs. prior periods.
Subsequent events review: check whether significant events after reporting date (e.g., impairment indicators, dividend declarations) affect valuation.
Detailed schedule of joint venture investments
General ledger and subsidiary ledger balances for JV accounts.
Reconciliation of JV balances with supporting schedules.
Accounting policies applied for recognition, measurement, and impairment of JVs.
Joint venture agreements or contracts specifying rights, obligations, and profit-sharing arrangements.
Board of Directors’ approvals/resolutions relating to JV formation or funding.
Share certificates, capital contribution documents, or partnership agreements proving ownership.
Financial statements of the JV (audited if available) to support equity method calculations.
Dividend declarations and receipts (bank evidence, JV distribution records).
Management’s equity method workings (calculation of share of profit/loss, adjustments, OCI, etc.).
Impairment assessment documentation if there are indications of reduced value.
Confirmation from JV management of ownership, balances, and distributions.
Extracts from legal or government registries verifying JV registration and ownership.
Market/valuation data if JV fair value disclosure is required.
Comparison of JV’s reported results with the investor’s share recorded in books.
Trend analysis of JV’s profitability and liquidity.
Subsequent events review: check significant developments after reporting date (impairment, capital calls, major contracts).
Tax computation and reconciliation between accounting profit and taxable income.
General ledger and subsidiary ledger balances for deferred tax accounts.
Accounting policy for deferred taxes (recognition, measurement, and offsetting).
Supporting calculations for each temporary difference (e.g., depreciation vs. tax depreciation, provisions, accruals, etc.).
Tax returns and filings (current and prior years) to confirm availability of tax losses or credits carried forward.
Correspondence with tax authorities (assessments, audits, rulings, disputes).
Board of Directors/management documentation on judgments and assumptions used for recognition of DTA.
Schedules of tax loss expiration dates and applicable tax regulations.
Confirmation of tax positions from external tax advisors (if management obtained one).
Tax authority regulations/guidance to verify eligibility of tax credits or carryforwards.
Industry/market data if external benchmarks are used in forecasting taxable profits.
Reconciliation of deferred tax movements: opening → additions → reversals → closing balance.
Comparison of tax rates applied with enacted/substantively enacted rates at reporting date.
Forecasts of future taxable profits (budgets, business plans, tax planning strategies) to assess recoverability of DTA.
Sensitivity analysis on key assumptions (growth rates, margins, utilization of tax losses).
Trend analysis: review historical ability of the company to use DTAs.
General ledger and subsidiary ledger balances for PPE.
Reconciliation between fixed asset register, general ledger, and financial statements.
Capitalization policy (thresholds, treatment of repairs vs. capital expenditures).
Depreciation schedules and calculations for the current year.
Impairment assessment documents if indicators exist.
Purchase invoices, contracts, or payment vouchers supporting asset acquisitions.
Title deeds, ownership certificates, or lease agreements (to verify ownership rights).
Construction contracts, progress reports, and budgets (for self-constructed assets).
Disposal documents (sales invoices, scrapping authorizations, board approvals).
Insurance policies covering major fixed assets.
Maintenance/repair records (to verify distinction between expenses and capitalized costs).
Physical inspection of assets (existence and condition verification).
External appraisals/valuations (if fair value model or revaluation model is applied).
Land/building registry extracts (for real estate ownership confirmation).
Third-party confirmations (e.g., leased assets, pledged assets under loan covenants).
Depreciation analysis: compare with prior years, check reasonableness of rates and methods.
Ratio and trend analysis: fixed asset turnover, depreciation % of gross PPE.
Comparison of capital expenditures with budgets and board-approved projects.
Subsequent events review: asset acquisitions, disposals, or impairments after year-end.
Company’s lease accounting policy (classification, discount rate policy, short-term/low-value exemptions).
Impairment assessment documents for ROU assets.
Lease agreements and contracts (including amendments, renewals, and termination clauses).
Payment records (bank statements, invoices, payment schedules) for lease rentals.
Supporting calculations for initial recognition (lease liability present value, initial direct costs, prepayments, restoration obligations).
Impairment test workings if indicators exist (e.g., lease modifications, idle assets).
Confirmation from lessors (if necessary) regarding lease terms, payments, or outstanding balances.
Property or asset registry extracts (if applicable, e.g., for property leases).
External appraisals or valuations if fair value is disclosed or impairment testing requires market inputs.
Comparison of depreciation expense with prior periods and with lease liability amortization.
Reconciliation between ROU asset amortization and lease liability reduction.
Trend analysis of lease-related ratios (lease expense vs. total expenses, ROU assets vs. total assets).
Subsequent events review: new leases, modifications, or early terminations after year-end.
General ledger and subsidiary ledger balances for intangibles.
Reconciliation between the register, general ledger, and financial statements.
Company’s capitalization policy (e.g., for internally developed software, R&D).
Impairment testing documentation (especially for goodwill and indefinite-life intangibles).
Purchase invoices, contracts, or licensing agreements for acquired intangibles.
Registration certificates or legal documents (patents, trademarks, copyrights).
Board/management approvals for acquisitions or internally developed projects.
R&D/project documentation for internally generated intangibles (proof of development phase vs. research phase).
Disposal records (sale contracts, expiry notices, abandonment approvals).
Legal correspondence related to disputes or challenges to rights (e.g., patent litigation).
Confirmations from licensing authorities or patent/trademark offices (validity and ownership).
Valuation reports from independent experts (if acquired in a business combination or fair value remeasurement).
Legal confirmations on pending disputes affecting rights.
Comparison of amortization expense against prior periods and expected useful lives.
Trend analysis: ratio of intangible assets to total assets, revenues supported by intangibles (e.g., software-driven sales).
Forecasts/cash flow projections (used in impairment testing).
Subsequent events review: expirations, renewals, or impairment indicators after year-end.
General ledger and subsidiary ledger balances for investment property.
Reconciliation of investment property register to the general ledger and financial statements.
Company’s accounting policy for investment property (cost vs. fair value).
Purchase agreements, invoices, and payment evidence for acquisitions.
Title deeds or legal ownership certificates for property ownership rights.
Lease agreements/contracts with tenants to verify rental income linkage.
Board/management approvals of property purchases or disposals.
Disposal documents (sale contracts, notarial deeds, transfer approvals).
Property management records (rental schedules, maintenance costs, insurance).
External property valuation reports (if applying fair value model or impairment testing).
Land/building registry extracts to confirm legal ownership and encumbrances (e.g., mortgages, pledges).
Confirmation from tenants (if material) for rental arrangements.
Market data for comparable property valuations.
Comparison of rental income with expected yields from properties.
Trend analysis of property valuations and rental income vs. prior periods.
Budget vs. actual analysis for rental income and property-related expenses.
Subsequent events review: significant sales, purchases, or revaluations after year-end.

Detailed schedule of Other Non-Current Assets, broken down by type (e.g., long-term advances, security deposits, long-term prepayments, deferred charges, assets under construction not classified as PPE, etc.).
General ledger and subsidiary ledger balances supporting ONCA.
Reconciliation of subsidiary records to the trial balance and financial statements.
Company’s accounting policies explaining what is classified as ONCA.
Deposit/guarantee agreements (e.g., rental deposits, utility deposits).
Advance payment contracts for long-term projects or suppliers.
Insurance or maintenance contracts for long-term prepaid expenses.
Project development agreements for construction-in-progress not yet transferred to PPE.
Deferred charge documentation (start-up costs, bond issuance costs, etc.).
Supporting calculations for amortization schedules of deferred costs.
Board of directors/management approvals for significant advances or long-term agreements.
Confirmation letters from counterparties (e.g., landlords, vendors, service providers) for deposits and advances.
Bank confirmations (if deposits are pledged as collateral).
Legal confirmations (for guarantees, pending litigations if included).
Market/third-party data if ONCA includes long-term investments not classified elsewhere.
Roll-forward schedule: Opening balance → additions → amortization/usage → transfers → closing balance.
Impairment assessment: evidence of recoverability for long-term advances or deposits.
Aging analysis: to ensure assets are genuinely long-term and not misclassified.
Comparison with prior periods for unusual increases/decreases.
Subsequent events review: repayments, settlements, or reclassifications after year-end.
Detailed trade payable listing by vendor, reconciled to the general ledger and financial statements.
Aging schedule of payables (to assess overdue amounts and completeness).
Trial balance and general ledger accounts related to trade payables.
Purchase journal / accounts payable sub-ledger for the period.
Company’s accounting policies on recognition of payables.
Purchase orders and goods received notes (GRNs) matched against invoices (three-way match).
Receiving reports or delivery notes for goods/services.
Contract agreements with suppliers, if relevant.
Payment vouchers and bank records for payables settled after year-end (subsequent disbursements).
Supplier/vendor confirmations of balances (positive or negative confirmations).
Bank confirmations to identify payments and outstanding obligations.
Legal confirmations for any supplier disputes or contingent liabilities.
Reconciliation: trade payable sub-ledger vs. general ledger.
Cutoff testing: review transactions before and after year-end to ensure liabilities are recorded in the correct period.
Comparative analysis: trade payables vs. purchases, COGS, inventory turnover.
Foreign currency revaluation schedules (if payables are denominated in foreign currency).
Detailed schedule of accruals and other payables, broken down by type (e.g., accrued expenses, accrued interest, payroll liabilities, utilities payable, customer advances, provisions).
General ledger and trial balance accounts supporting accruals and other payables.
Company’s accounting policies on accruals and payable recognition.
Roll-forward schedule (opening balance → additions → payments → reversals → closing balance).
Accrual calculations and estimates prepared by management (e.g., payroll accrual, utilities accrual, bonus accrual, interest accrual).
Contracts, agreements, or loan documents for interest and other periodic obligations.
Payroll records and HR documentation for accrued salaries and bonuses.
Utility bills, service agreements, or invoices received after year-end to validate accruals.
Board/management meeting minutes approving bonuses, provisions, or significant accruals.
Tax authority correspondence if the account includes accrued taxes.
Confirmation letters for accrued interest or other borrowings from banks/creditors.
Legal confirmations for accrued legal fees, settlements, or other contingent payables.
Vendor statements for services rendered but not yet invoiced.
Cut-off testing: review expenses incurred before year-end but invoiced/paid after year-end.
Subsequent payments testing: trace payments after the reporting date to see if they relate to accrued liabilities.
Comparison with prior year accruals (consistency check for recurring accruals like utilities, interest, payroll).
Reconciliation of balances with related accounts (e.g., payroll accruals vs. payroll expense).
Detailed schedule of contract liabilities, reconciled to the general ledger and trial balance.
Breakdown by contract/customer/project, showing opening balance → additions (customer prepayments, billings) → revenue recognized → closing balance.
Revenue recognition policies and procedures applied by management
Reconciliation between contract liabilities and deferred revenue accounts.
Invoices/billing documents issued before performance obligations are satisfied.
Customer receipts/prepayment records (bank statements, cash receipts journal).
Delivery notes, service completion reports, or project progress certificates showing whether obligations were satisfied at year-end.
Management’s revenue recognition workings, including percentage-of-completion or stage-of-delivery analysis, where relevant.
Credit notes or contract modifications that affect liabilities.
Customer confirmations for advances, deposits, or unearned revenue balances.
Bank confirmations showing restricted cash balances (if contract liabilities are linked to advance deposits).
Legal confirmations for contracts with unusual terms or ongoing disputes.
Cut-off testing: review sales transactions before and after year-end to ensure proper timing of revenue vs. contract liability recognition.
Subsequent events testing: verify whether contract liabilities were satisfied after year-end and properly reduced.
Comparisons: vs. prior year balances (trend analysis); vs. sales, backlog, and customer advances.
Reasonableness testing: check whether contract liabilities align with customer advances, project milestones, and industry practices.
General ledger and trial balance showing overdraft balances.
Bank overdraft schedule, detailing each overdraft facility (bank, account number, currency, interest rate, maturity, collateral, covenants).
Cash book / bank book reconciliation with overdraft balances.
Company’s accounting policy on presentation (netting vs. gross, classification as current liability).
Bank statements at and around year-end showing overdraft balances.
Correspondence with banks on facility renewals, breaches, or waivers.
Board/management approvals for overdraft facility arrangements.
Legal confirmations if overdrafts are subject to disputes or guarantees.
Bank reconciliations prepared by management, including outstanding checks and deposits in transit.
Subsequent cash flows: review whether overdrafts were repaid or further utilized after year-end.
Comparison with prior year overdrafts: identify unusual fluctuations.
Interest expense reconciliation: check interest charged by banks vs. amounts recorded in P&L.
Facility utilization analysis: compare actual overdraft use vs. approved limit.
Foreign currency revaluation schedules (if overdrafts are in foreign currency).
Detailed schedule of provisions, by type (legal cases, restructuring, environmental, warranty, penalties, etc.).
General ledger and trial balance supporting provision balances.
Roll-forward schedule (opening balance → additions → utilizations → reversals → closing balance).
Company’s accounting policies on provisions and contingent liabilities.
Management’s estimation workings used to calculate the provision (assumptions, models, percentages).
Contracts/agreements giving rise to obligations (warranty terms, service agreements, construction contracts).
Internal reports on restructuring plans, redundancy notices, or environmental remediation plans.
Correspondence and claim letters from counterparties, regulators, or customers.
Board of directors/management approvals for restructuring, litigation settlements, or major provisions.
Calculations and actuarial reports (if provisions involve estimates like environmental or long-term obligations).
Invoices or claims settled after year-end (subsequent events) that validate the existence/amount of provision.
Legal confirmations from the company’s lawyers regarding ongoing or threatened litigations and their likelihood of loss.
Expert/consultant reports (e.g., engineers for environmental liabilities, actuaries for warranty/reserve calculations).
Regulatory correspondence confirming fines, compliance obligations, or environmental cleanup requirements.
Reasonableness testing: compare provision levels against: prior years, industry peers, etc.
Subsequent events review: determine if provisions recognized were settled after year-end and whether amounts were reasonable.
Trend analysis: unusual increases/decreases in provisions compared with related expenses (e.g., warranty provision vs. sales trends).
Sensitivity analysis: impact of changes in assumptions on provision amounts.
Detailed schedule of employee benefit liabilities, broken down by type (wages payable, bonus payable, vacation accrual, social security, pension contributions, etc.).
General ledger and trial balance balances for employee benefit liabilities.
Roll-forward schedule (opening balance → accruals → payments → reversals → closing balance).
Company’s accounting policies on recognition of employee benefits and accruals.
Payroll records and payroll journal entries for the year.
Employment contracts and collective bargaining agreements (salary, bonus, overtime, leave entitlements).
Payroll registers (gross pay, deductions, net pay).
Bonus/commission plans and board of directors’ approvals for declared bonuses.
Time records/attendance logs supporting wages accrued at year-end.
Government regulations on mandatory contributions (e.g., pension, health insurance, social security).
Invoices and filings for social security/tax contributions.
Subsequent payments records (bank transfers, payroll disbursements after year-end).
Bank confirmations for unpaid payroll or contributions deducted but not yet remitted.
Confirmations with government agencies (if feasible) for unpaid contributions or tax withholdings.
Third-party confirmations for payroll service providers (if outsourced).
Cut-off testing: check December/January payroll transactions to ensure proper year-end accrual.
Subsequent disbursement review: verify liabilities cleared in the following month(s).
Reasonableness checks: Compare accrued salaries with number of unpaid days at year-end × daily payroll.; Compare accrued bonuses with approved bonus pool and profitability trends.
Trend analysis: compare current year accruals with prior year and with headcount growth/salary increases.
Reconciliation: employee benefit liabilities vs. payroll expense recognized.
Detailed schedule of taxes payable, broken down by type (corporate income tax, VAT, withholding taxes, payroll tax, excise, etc.).
General ledger balances for taxes payable and tax expense accounts.
Tax computation worksheets prepared by management, reconciling book profit to taxable profit.
Roll-forward of tax liabilities (opening balance → accruals/charges → payments → adjustments → closing balance).
Accounting policies relating to tax accruals and recognition.
Trial balance and journal entries related to tax accruals, tax payments, and adjustments.
Filed tax returns (corporate income tax, VAT returns, payroll/withholding tax reports).
Tax assessment letters or correspondence with tax authorities.
Supporting schedules for temporary and permanent differences between accounting income and taxable income.
Board of directors’ minutes/approvals for tax settlement decisions or disputes.
Payment vouchers and bank transfer records for tax remittances.
Confirmations with tax authorities (if feasible or required) regarding outstanding balances, assessments, or disputes.
Lawyer’s letters regarding tax litigation or disputes.
External tax consultant reports if the company uses advisors for tax calculations or disputes.
Cut-off testing: review December/January transactions to ensure correct period recognition.
Subsequent payment review: check whether outstanding year-end liabilities were paid in the following months.
Reconciliation: Tax expense per books vs. tax payable accruals; Tax payable vs. amounts reported in filed tax returns.
Reasonableness checks: Effective tax rate analysis (tax expense ÷ accounting profit).; Comparison with statutory tax rates.
Trend analysis: compare current year’s payable balance with prior years, considering profitability and tax regulations.
Detailed listing of liabilities included in the disposal group (e.g., loans, payables, provisions, employee obligations, lease liabilities).
Management’s disposal plan approved by the board/management (including evidence of commitment to sell within 12 months).
General ledger balances for liabilities transferred to the disposal group.
Roll-forward schedule showing movement of these liabilities (opening balance, additions, reclassifications, payments, closing balance).
Contracts/agreements related to the planned disposal (e.g., sale agreements, letters of intent, binding offers, memoranda of understanding).
Board of directors’ or shareholders’ resolutions approving the disposal.
Legal documents relating to liabilities transferred (loan agreements, lease contracts, supplier contracts).
Breakdown and supporting schedules for each liability class included in the disposal group.
Correspondence with creditors or counterparties about settlement/transfer of liabilities.
Confirmation from buyers/investors (if applicable) on assumption of liabilities in the disposal.
Bank confirmations for loans included in the disposal group.
Supplier/creditor confirmations for trade or non-trade payables classified in the disposal group.
Legal letters regarding litigation or contingent liabilities tied to the disposal group.
